questions.q: What is a "line of symmetry" in a building or piece of art?
questions.a: A line of symmetry is an imaginary line that divides a figure into two identical halves that perfectly overlap if folded. A wrong answer like "a line that cuts an object into two parts" is incomplete because it ignores the requirement that the parts must be mirror images/identical.

questions.q: If you look at the front of a rectangular building with a door exactly in the center, why do we say it is symmetric?
questions.a: It is symmetric because the vertical line passing through the center of the door creates two sides that are mirror reflections of each other. A student who says "because it's a rectangle" misses the point; a rectangle is symmetric, but the architecture's symmetry depends on the placement of features like the door and windows relative to that central line.

questions.q: If a square-shaped courtyard has a pattern that looks the same after a 90-degree turn, does it have rotational symmetry?
questions.a: Yes, because it returns to its original appearance after a partial rotation. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses rotational symmetry with line symmetry; they are testing for "look-alike" positions after turning, not folding.

questions.q: Compare the symmetry of a circle to the symmetry of a triangle. How do they differ?
questions.a: A circle has an infinite number of lines of symmetry (every diameter), whereas a triangle (depending on its type) has a fixed, small number (0, 1, or 3). A student failing to mention the difference in the *number* of lines shows they haven't grasped that symmetry is a measurable property.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "All symmetric buildings must have exactly two lines of symmetry." Is this true?
questions.a: This is false; buildings can have one line (like many houses), four lines (like a square-based structure), or even none if the architecture is asymmetrical. A student agreeing with the statement likely hasn't looked at diverse examples and assumes symmetry is limited to a single "cross" shape.

questions.q: Create a plan for a simple garden path pattern that has at least two lines of symmetry.
questions.a: A good response describes a square or rectangular layout where items (like flower beds) are placed at equal distances from a horizontal and vertical center. A poor answer just says "make it pretty" without explaining the placement relative to the center lines.
